newsitem.title: UK: Candidates line up to replace Major after UK poll.
newsitem.headline: Candidates line up to replace Major after UK poll.

text.p: Britain's quarrelsome Conservatives, whose feuds paved the road to last week's electoral disaster, have plunged straight into a struggle of survivors over the party leadership.

Their choice of a successor to defeated prime minister John Major gives open display to policy and personal differences that were rarely better than half hidden as their 18 years of power drew to a close.

Last week's crushing defeat cut down the field, winnowing out former defence secretary Michael Portillo -- a pre-poll favourite -- and former foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind, who both lost their seats.
Major's deputy, Michael Heseltine, 64, lost his chance when he was rushed to hospital with heart problems.
Hong Kong governor Chris Patten, a close ally of Major, has ruled himself out, dismissing conspiracy theorists who saw him returning to the House of Commons to fight for the leadership.

The final list -- barring late surprises -- comprises six former ministers. First away was John Redwood, 45, a former Welsh secretary who two years ago accepted Major's leadership challenge designed to end the party's splits over Europe.
Redwood's defeat did little to dent his ambition, which he nursed in the run up to the election with repeated calls for a tougher line against Brussels and a European single currency.
But the Conservative party places a premium on loyalty and Redwood's decision to challenge Major could count against him.
Another contender for the right-wing vote is former home secretary, Michael Howard, 55.
His tough "hang 'em and flog 'em" rhetoric won support from the right of the party as did his hostile tone on Europe. But he has to overcome a shifty image.

Another former Welsh secretary, William Hague, was the latest to join the race on Wednesday -- after a very public falling out with Howard who accused him of breaking a late night deal sealed with champagne to stand as Howard's deputy.
Hague took the Conservative Party conference by storm with a bravura speech while still in his teens. Now 36, he is still seen as a boy wonder with a relative lack of experience.
The same cannot be said of the main contender on the left -- former chancellor of the exchequer Kenneth Clarke, 56, one of the sharpest parliamentary performers.
But he angered Eurosceptics by defending his pro-European line in cabinet and preventing Major ruling out entry into a single currency. His appointment could split the party.
That leaves Stephen Dorrell, 45, former health secretary.

He has been described as the Conservative mirror-image of Labour leader Tony Blair in that both are boyish, socially concerned, intellectual -- a good selling point for a job which will pit any new Conservative leader against Blair.

Peter Lilley, one of four Thatcherite right-wing cabinet members famously dubbed "bastards" in an off-the-cuff remark by John Major, made his mark at Conservative party conferences with rabble-rousing speeches attacking Europe and single mothers.
As social security secretary, Lilley chipped away at the 85 billion pound ($139 billion) annual budget of Britain's welfare state.
But -- despite the support of Gillian Shephard, the former Education and Employment Secretary and originally seen as a potential compromise candidate -- he is not a favourite.
The contest will be run by the so-called 1922 Committee which groups rank-and-file Conservative members of parliament.
First, however, it has to find its own new leader to replace veteran chairman Sir Marcus Fox who lost his seat last week. Voting for the party leadership is due on Tuesday, June 3.
A winner needs a minimum of 50 percent of the 165 Conservative MPs who made it into the House of Commons and a margin of 15 percent over the second placed candidate.
If there is no outright winner, new contenders can join in the race and a second ballot will be held on June 10. The winner would need 50 percent, but not a 15 percent winning margin.
If necessary a third ballot would be held two days later between the top two candidates with a simple majority to decide.
